query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the selective oxidation of elements with high oxygen affinity (especially Al and to some extent Cr) governs the formation of a dense, coherent oxide scale at temperatures above 900 °C. When the alloy contains sufficient Al, it forms a continuous, slow-growing Al2O3 (often assisted by Cr2O3) that acts as an effective diffusion barrier, whereas alloys where X is Si or Mn (which do not form similarly protective oxides) develop heterogeneous, porous oxides that crack or spall.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a stabilized single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Exposure to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (above 900 °C) in an oxidative/corrosive environment; controlled variation of the X element (Al, Si, or Mn) while maintaining similar baseline compositions; testing performed on alloys in their as-processed solid-solution state.
generation.structural_mediator: Development of a dense, continuous Al2O3/Cr2O3 oxide scale that limits oxygen diffusion and minimizes interfacial stress.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism is based on selective oxidation: sufficient Al (and Cr) preferentially oxidizes to form stable, adherent oxide scales with minimal growth stress. In contrast, when X is Si or Mn, the resulting oxide phases are less protective due to lower film density and higher growth stresses, leading to cracking or spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with higher Al content will form a stable, coherent oxide layer that persists during prolonged exposure above 900 °C, while those with predominantly Si or Mn as the variable element will exhibit unstable, discontinuous oxides that crack or spall under the same conditions.
generation.baseline: A comparable CrFeCoNiX alloy with limited Al (or with X = Si or Mn) is expected to form a less protective oxide scale under identical high-temperature oxidative conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to exposures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, and to alloys maintained in a stabilized single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state.
generation.uncertainty: The precise roles and potential synergistic effects of Si and Mn in modifying the oxidation behaviour remain less well understood, requiring further quantitative studies to define critical composition thresholds for protective scale formation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize CrFeCoNiX alloys with controlled variations where X = Al, Si, or Mn while keeping other elements and processing conditions constant. Expose these samples to oxidative atmospheres at temperatures above 900 °C for fixed durations, then analyze the surface oxide morphology and composition.
measurements: Surface oxide morphology and continuity via scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
Phase composition of the oxide scales using X-ray diffraction (XRD)
Elemental distribution and segregation in the oxide layers using energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
Adhesion strength of the oxide scales through mechanical scratch testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if alloys with high Al content do not consistently exhibit a denser, more coherent and adherent oxide layer compared to those with X = Si or Mn, or if no significant differences in oxide scale stability and protective behaviour are observed under identical testing conditions.

## Abstract
AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition
